headline: Morocco names its first woman prime minister
summary: King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra Mansouri prime minister on Tuesday, the first woman to hold the job in Morocco. She is 50, a lawyer, and the mayor of Marrakech. Her party won the most seats last week, so by the constitution the king had to pick from it. Now she needs a coalition: her party has 97 seats, and a majority is 198.

cover_question.q: Why does the king get to pick?

cover_answer: He has to. From the party that won the most seats.
table_question: If you won the vote but someone else had to sign off, did you win?

5-7.script: A country called Morocco picked a new leader for its government today, and for the first time ever it's a woman. Her name is Fatima Zahra Mansouri. She was the mayor of a city called Marrakech, so it's like the captain of one team getting asked to run the whole league. Good news, and that's the whole story.
5-7.why: One name, one city, one first. That is as much as this age needs.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them one: a woman got the top job for the first time. The mayor-to-league captain comparison makes the step up something they can picture. Expect "can a girl be president here?" Yes, though none has been yet, and that is an honest place to leave it.

8-12.script: Last week Morocco voted, and Fatima Zahra Mansouri's party won the most seats. The king picks the prime minister, but since 2011 he must pick from the party that came first. On Tuesday he named her, the first woman in the job. A referee makes the call, but the rule book says which side gets it.
8-12.why: Vote, rule, pick: a chain they can test.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out how rules bind the people at the top: a king who chooses, and a 2011 rule that says where from. The script hands them the chain, and the referee shows a call that is still his but no longer free. Expect "so the king could have said no?" Not to the party. To her, yes: he passed over the football chief.

13-17.script: Is it a win for women if the king still holds most of the power? Morocco's king named Fatima Zahra Mansouri prime minister, the first woman in the job. He had to choose from her party, a rule protesters won in 2011. Second: she rarely talks about women's rights. Does a first owe the ones after anything?
13-17.why: Two real questions, no settled answer.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a first for women, and a king who kept most of the power. The script hands them both, then a harder pair: Mansouri rarely speaks about women's rights, and she is the one who broke through. Expect "would she have got it without the 2011 rule?" Nobody knows. The party still had to win.

5-7.a: The person who runs the government day to day. In Morocco a king is above the prime minister, and he picks who gets the job.

8-12.q: Why does the king get to pick?
8-12.a: The constitution says so. Since 2011, only from the winning party.
Not yet. 97 of 395 seats, and she needs 198. So, partners.

13-17.q: Is it a real win if the king keeps most power?
13-17.a: Most power stays with the king. But he had to pick from the winning party.

13-17.q: Why has this taken so long in Arab countries?
13-17.a: The articles don't say. She's only the second, after Tunisia's.
